## 1. Shift summary

The past shift was mostly steady across regions, with no prolonged disruptions or deep platform degradations to chase down. We had a pair of short external bumps touch our edge and email alerting, but both cleared quickly once upstream systems stabilized. Routine tasks and background processes finished without trouble, leaving the fleet in clean shape for the coming rotation.

## 2. What happened

The following items came up across the week and were addressed as noted:

- On Monday, we saw API-2502 for one partner's calendar sync on Monday: their sync token expired after they changed the password on their side. They reconnected; nothing for us to do. Because the issue was tied entirely to their credentials refresh and resolved cleanly once they re-authenticated, the chosen handling was no action on our end.
- On Wednesday 2026-07-01, web-cdn-edge reached 2.9 % for 6 minutes on Wednesday 2026-07-01; the cloudflare status page showed an incident at one edge location. First move: check provider. The metrics tool caught the momentary lift, but traffic normalized as soon as the provider resolved routing at that specific edge site, requiring no further intervention from us.
- On Friday 2026-07-03, notifier-email-fail touched 24 % for 6 minutes on Friday 2026-07-03; the sendgrid status page showed delayed processing. First move: check provider. It cleared with nothing changed on our side. Delivery rates recovered back to baseline levels immediately after the external delay passed.
- Over the weekend, the scheduled settlement run executed cleanly. The Sunday payout job ran at 23:00 JST and finished in 34 minutes. Batches proceeded without dropped records or stalled worker processes across the ledger.

## 3. Service status

- web: Pointing back to what happened with web-cdn-edge reaching 2.9 % on Wednesday 2026-07-01 during the cloudflare edge issue, otherwise normal.
- api: Pointing back to what happened with API-2502 on Monday for the partner calendar sync credential reset, otherwise normal.
- payments: Normal, pointing back to what happened with the Sunday payout job running at 23:00 JST and finishing in 34 minutes.
- notifier: Pointing back to what happened with notifier-email-fail touching 24 % on Friday 2026-07-03 during the sendgrid processing delay, otherwise normal.

## 4. Notes for the incoming on-call

- Keep an eye on external dependencies early in the rotation; both alerts that fired this week originated on vendor infrastructure rather than inside our own application code.
- Remember the standard five options for alerts: roll back, read logs, check provider, page owner, or no action. When an alert metric spikes sharply without recent service deploys, check provider first if the monitor tracks an integrated gateway.
- You can watch the respective boards ("Sorrel / web", "Sorrel / api", "Sorrel / payments", and "Sorrel / notifier") if anything unusual begins drifting during business hours.
- If an alert triggers where nobody knows yet what happened, use the log search tool over sorrel-prod-* to read logs before taking disruptive steps.
- If you run into situations where state cannot be reversed or decisions fall outside SRE remit, page owner directly using the paging tool.
- Regional routing across ap-northeast, us-east, and eu-west has remained well-balanced through the weekend.
- The queue for background jobs in notifier and payments is clear heading into Monday morning.

## 5. Sign-off

Handing over the rotation now to Noor. The handover is finished when the incoming on-call writes "taken" in #inc-live.

Sara  
Outgoing on-call

# On-call handover, week of 2026-07-20

Last updated: 2026-07-20 10:00 JST  
Author: Priya (web), outgoing on-call  
Incoming on-call: Leo (payments)  

## 1. Shift summary

The shift was mostly manageable, though Wednesday morning kept us busy across two services at the same time. Outside of an upstream payment gateway blip and a session stampede on web, the core infrastructure behaved itself across all three regions. Leo takes over the rotation with no outstanding rollbacks pending from my week.

## 2. What happened

A few specific events required attention during the rotation:

* Deploys this week: web 2, api 2, payments 1, notifier 1; all in the Tuesday and Thursday afternoon windows. None of these scheduled releases ran into issues or caused alerts during their rollout windows.
* Token refresh stampede on Wednesday at 09:00 JST: every web session issued before the signing key rotation expired at the same moment, so everyone had to sign in again at once and sign-in p95 went to 9 s for 14 minutes. Priya added jitter so session expiry is spread out from now on. The load dropped back down as soon as the renewed tokens settled across user sessions.
* api-partner-reject fired for one partner on Wednesday 2026-07-15 at 10:28 JST: the partner ran a full re-sync and hit its contracted limit. First move: read logs. Once we pulled the context from the log search tool, Ravi confirmed the limit stays as it is, so no further configuration adjustments were made on the api tier.
* payments-provider-timeout fired on Thursday 2026-07-16 at 20:10 JST; the stripe status page reported degraded API performance; cleared in 25 minutes. First move: check provider. Because the failure was isolated to their external processing layer, we monitored the recovery until their health indicators stabilized and the alert resolved cleanly.

## 3. Service status

* web: Degraded on Wednesday during the token refresh stampede; currently normal.
* api: Raised an alert during the partner re-sync limit hit on Wednesday 2026-07-15; currently normal.
* payments: Elevated timeouts during the stripe performance degradation on Thursday 2026-07-16; currently normal.
* notifier: Normal throughout the shift.

## 4. Notes for the incoming on-call

Keep an eye on the boards and the paging tool during the standard release windows on Tuesday and Thursday afternoon. 

The web layer should no longer suffer from synchronized expirations following the jitter fix deployed after Wednesday's stampede, but watch login latency trends if another key rotation is scheduled. For third-party errors, remember that provider status pages often show root causes before internal traces can isolate them, exactly as we saw with the stripe degradation on Thursday. If partner queries spike unexpectedly on api, check the queries in the logs before escalating, as partners frequently run heavy re-sync batches that bump right against their existing contracted ceilings.

All standard boards remain healthy heading into the new week.

## 5. Sign-off

Handing over the primary pager to Leo. Handover completes once Leo posts "taken" in #inc-live.

Author: Leo (payments), outgoing on-call  
Incoming on-call: Yuki (notifier)  

## 1. Shift summary

The rotation was mostly quiet this week with only two alerts firing during the shift. Both events were handled quickly without direct user impact, one clearing cleanly after upstream recovery and the other requiring no immediate intervention. Overall platform health remained steady across all regions, and no Sev incidents were opened.

## 2. What happened

The following items came through the paging tool during the rotation:

* **payments-provider-timeout alert on Wednesday 2026-07-22:**
  * Fired at 20:52 JST.
  * The first move taken was check provider, as the alert pointed to our external payment processing layer.
  * Looked at outside dependencies, and the stripe status page reported degraded API performance.
  * The condition resolved on their side, and the alert cleared in 18 minutes.
  * Verified that charge and refund processing settled back to expected baselines once their systems stabilized.

* **web-traffic alert on Saturday 2026-07-25:**
  * Fired at 14:34 JST.
  * Checked traffic patterns and confirmed this was caused by a search-engine crawler on public business pages.
  * Volume reached about 3.8x the same hour last week, but the service handled the requests cleanly with all 2xx responses.
  * Because nothing had failed and no customer was affected, the first move taken was no action.
  * Logged a ticket for Aiko about crawler limits so the web team can evaluate rate limiting policies on those routes when appropriate.

* **Customer support escalation volume:**
  * Support (Hana) had a quiet week: no escalations to on-call.
  * No customer-facing issues required engineering escalation, hotfixes, or manual account corrections during this shift.

## 3. Service status

* **web**: Normal; handled elevated public business page crawler traffic on Saturday without errors.
* **api**: Normal; ran without incidents or paging alerts throughout the shift.
* **payments**: Normal; transient timeout alert on Wednesday resolved after provider recovered.
* **notifier**: Normal; message delivery ran cleanly all week with no alerts.

## 4. Notes for the incoming on-call

A few items to keep in mind for Yuki taking over the pager:

* Monitor external dependencies if payment timeouts resurface. Wednesday showed that provider dips can trigger alerts briefly before clearing on their own, so checking upstream dashboards first remains the right path.
* Keep an eye out for any further spikes from web crawlers hitting public business listings. While the backend scaled through Saturday's load without dropping requests or elevating latencies, Aiko will likely follow up on crawler thresholds during normal hours.
* Keep standard channels open. Routine questions typically come via Hana from the support side, but with zero escalations this past week, backlogs are clear heading into Monday.

* Remember that the shift handover is finished when the incoming on-call writes "taken" in #inc-live.

Handing over the primary pager to Yuki. All four services are operating normally across ap-northeast, us-east, and eu-west. Good luck with the shift, and drop a line in the channel if anything strange turns up in the logs.

— Leo

## 2. What happened

## 3. Service status

- **web:** Pointing back to what happened: had an isolated OOM node replacement on Tuesday in us-east and elevated crawler volume on Wednesday; currently normal.

- The handover is complete once Daniel acknowledges in the channel.

## 5. Sign-off

Handing over to Daniel. Please post "taken" in #inc-live once you have reviewed this page and assumed the paging tool rotation.

Last updated: 2026-08-10 10:00 JST  
Owner: Daniel (api), outgoing on-call  
Incoming on-call: Sara (platform)  

## 1. Shift summary

The week was generally quiet with no severe service degradation across any region. We handled two low-level alert events and a small batch of log noise, none of which caused user-facing impact or required paging service owners. All core flows across bookings, payouts, and notifications operated within acceptable operational boundaries throughout the shift.

## 2. What happened

A few operational events required verification over the course of the week:

- A few NTF-3460 log lines on Tuesday: reminders dropped as duplicates by the dedupe key after a worker retried. Expected; no customer missed a reminder. I checked the logs simply to confirm deduplication behavior matched the queue worker's retry expectations, and the count remained negligible with no delivery gaps observed.
- web-4xx at 1.5 % for 12 minutes on Thursday 2026-08-06: an old marketing link pointing at a removed page. First move: read logs; no customer reports; ticket filed. The elevated response rate dropped back down naturally once the external referer traffic tapered off, and the missing route does not impact any current booking or admin workflows.
- notifier-queue-depth fired at Friday 2026-08-07 03:17 JST during the nightly reminder batch in ap-northeast (peak 1230 messages); delivered per minute stayed normal and the queue drained before 05:00. First move: no action. Processing throughput kept pace with the transient ingestion spike without worker stalling, so no manual queue intervention or scale adjustments were necessary.
- Support (Hana) had a quiet week: no escalations to on-call. Ticket inflow on their end did not surface any underlying edge cases requiring SRE or engineering investigation.

## 3. Service status

- web: Normal, brief 4xx bump on Thursday 2026-08-06 cleared without issue.
- api: Normal throughout the shift.
- payments: Normal throughout the shift.
- notifier: Normal, transient queue depth spike on Friday 2026-08-07 and isolated dedupe lines on Tuesday resolved as expected.

## 4. Notes for the incoming on-call

- The web 4xx ticket filed on Thursday covers the legacy route redirect cleanup; there is no immediate action required unless marketing reactivates external campaigns pointing to dead URLs.
- The notifier queue buildup in ap-northeast was entirely batch-driven; monitor the early morning reminder runs if message volumes grow further, but standard throughput is handling the load adequately.
- Keep an eye on incoming alerts in the standard channels, and confirm handover completion in the operational room.

## 5. Sign-off

Handing off primary on-call duties to Sara. Handover complete once Sara writes "taken" in #inc-live.

— Daniel

Hard rules:
- Use every fact you are given, with every number, name, code, config key and date exactly as written. Add no new
  facts: no new incidents, numbers, error codes, config keys, partner names or people. You may add connecting words,
  a one-line judgement from the author, and a routine sign-off.
- Keep the team's own words for things exactly as the facts give them; do not explain a term in other words and do not
  add a plain-language gloss.

  only if a fact does, and then only as the fact says, with no commands.

What the team works with:
Sorrel is a scheduling app (salons, clinics, tutors book appointments through it). Four services: web
(pages and the admin tool), api (businesses, bookings, search, the partner API, the audit log), payments (charges,
refunds, weekly payouts to businesses), notifier (email and SMS). Regions: ap-northeast, us-east, eu-west.
Owners: Aiko (web), Ravi (api), Mei (payments), Tom (notifier). Others: Kenji Sato (platform lead), Sara (platform
engineer), Hana (support lead), Daniel (api engineer), Yuki (notifier engineer), Priya (web engineer), Leo (payments
engineer), Noor (SRE, joined the rotation in April 2026). Providers: stripe (cards), twilio (SMS), sendgrid (email),

Last updated: 2026-09-14 10:00 JST  
Author: Yuki (notifier), outgoing on-call  
Incoming on-call: Noor (SRE)  

## 1. Shift summary

The week was mostly quiet across all regions with no major platform incidents or user-facing service interruptions. Two actionable alerts fired during the rotation, but both resolved quickly without requiring manual service intervention or rollbacks. We had zero escalations from Hana in support, leaving the rotation focused on routine monitoring and ticket triage.

## 2. What happened

A detailed log of the events and alerts raised during the shift:

- web-traffic fired on Wednesday 2026-09-09 at 14:31 JST: a search-engine crawler on public business pages, about 3.6x the same hour last week, all 2xx. First move: no action; ticket for Aiko about crawler limits. Traffic hit the edge and public landing views heavily, but backend error rates stayed flat and the host capacity handled the volume without degradation. Because all responses were successful and no customer traffic was impeded, no operational intervention was necessary on the cluster. Logged the traffic profile and left the ticket on the board for the service owner.
- payments-provider-timeout fired on Saturday 2026-09-12 at 20:53 JST; the stripe status page reported degraded API performance; cleared in 12 minutes. First move: check provider. Outbound requests from our processors had elevated latency during the window, matching the upstream degradation reported by the vendor. Watched the error counts and connection states until upstream throughput recovered and the alert resolved automatically.
- Support (Hana) had a quiet week: no escalations to on-call. Ticket volume in user channels remained manageable throughout normal clinic and salon scheduling hours, and zero tickets were escalated up to engineering or the primary rotation.

## 3. Service status

Current operational health across the core services:

- web: Normal; traffic returned to expected baselines following the crawler event on Wednesday.
- api: Normal; consistent latency and request rates across business booking and search endpoints.
- payments: Normal; provider latency returned to baseline after Saturday's upstream degradation.
- notifier: Normal; queue depths and message deliveries steady across all customer notifications.

## 4. Notes for the incoming on-call

A few items to keep in mind for Noor heading into the next rotation:

- Aiko has the crawler ticket queued, so keep an eye out if additional aggressive scraping runs hit the public endpoints prior to any edge rules being added.
- The metrics tool and log search tool dashboards are clean across ap-northeast, us-east, and eu-west.
- Pager notifications are routed as expected; confirm your paging tool schedule is active.
- Hana and the support team have no open items waiting on SRE input, so standard response channels remain the primary contact point.
- When you are ready to formally assume the rotation, acknowledge the transfer in the main channel to finalize the handoff.

## 5. Sign-off

Handing over primary responsibilities to Noor for the coming week. The shift is complete once Noor writes "taken" in #inc-live.

Yuki

parts.text:
You write internal pages for the SRE team of Sorrel. Write ONE page in Markdown, plain and realistic,
the way a small, busy SRE team writes: specific, a little dry, short sections, bullets where they help, no marketing
tone, no summary of what the page is for. Length: 550 to 700 words; do not stop short.
Sections, in this order, with numbered '## ' headings in the house style ('## 1. Shift summary'):
shift summary (two or three sentences, the author's view of the week); what happened (each fact, with the author's
plain account of what was seen and done); a one-line-per-service status for web, api, payments and notifier (normal,
or pointing back to what happened; no new numbers); notes for the incoming on-call; sign-off.

Start with exactly the header lines you are given, unchanged. Then write the body.

Hard rules:
- Use every fact you are given, with every number, name, code, config key and date exactly as written. Add no new
  facts: no new incidents, numbers, error codes, config keys, partner names or people. You may add connecting words,
  a one-line judgement from the author, and a routine sign-off.
- Keep the team's own words for things exactly as the facts give them; do not explain a term in other words and do not
  add a plain-language gloss.
- An error code (like ABC-1234) appears only where a fact puts it, written in passing inside a sentence. Never put an
  error code in a heading, a table header or the first line of a section.
- Never give rollback steps or rollback commands for any service. Never mention a tool called dtool. Mention Shipyard
  only if a fact does, and then only as the fact says, with no commands.
- No phone numbers, account ids, email addresses or URLs. Do not mention on-call pay, allowances or contracts.
- Do not copy alert rules or thresholds into tables, and do not write lists of 'for this alert, the first move is X'.
- Everything in the page happens on or before the page's date.

What the team works with:
Sorrel is a scheduling app (salons, clinics, tutors book appointments through it). Four services: web
(pages and the admin tool), api (businesses, bookings, search, the partner API, the audit log), payments (charges,
refunds, weekly payouts to businesses), notifier (email and SMS). Regions: ap-northeast, us-east, eu-west.
Owners: Aiko (web), Ravi (api), Mei (payments), Tom (notifier). Others: Kenji Sato (platform lead), Sara (platform
engineer), Hana (support lead), Daniel (api engineer), Yuki (notifier engineer), Priya (web engineer), Leo (payments
engineer), Noor (SRE, joined the rotation in April 2026). Providers: stripe (cards), twilio (SMS), sendgrid (email),
cloudflare (CDN and firewall), aws (hosting). The incident channel is #inc-live; boards are "Sorrel / web",
"Sorrel / api", "Sorrel / payments", "Sorrel / notifier"; logs are searched in sorrel-prod-*; people use the paging
tool, the metrics tool, the log search tool and the deploy tool. Severities: P1, P2, P3. A handover is finished when
the incoming on-call writes "taken" in #inc-live.

The five actions on-call chooses from:
At this company the five actions mean:
- roll back: undo the most recent deploy, when that deploy is recent enough to be the cause.
- read logs: go and read the service's own output, when nobody knows yet what happened.
- check provider: look at an outside service we depend on, when the alert already points at one.
- page owner: wake the person who owns this service, when something has already happened that you cannot undo - data seen, money moved, accounts deleted - or when somebody has to make a decision you are not allowed to make.
- no action: write it down and move on, when nothing has failed and no customer is affected.

# On-call handover, week of 2026-09-28

Date: 2026-09-28  
Owner: Leo (payments), outgoing on-call  
Incoming on-call: Leo (payments), second week in a row (swapped with Daniel)  

## 1. Shift summary

A fairly quiet week overall with only two alerts firing on web during Thursday afternoon. The rest of the platform ran cleanly across all regions, and payouts closed out the cycle on Sunday night without friction. Handing over to myself for a second consecutive shift so continuity should be straightforward.

## 2. What happened

- On Thursday 2026-09-24, web-node-restart fired for one us-east web node following two restarts in 30 minutes, out of memory. First move: read logs in sorrel-prod-* to understand what was exhausting memory on the host. The node was replaced and us-east capacity stabilized immediately afterward without further memory pressure.
- Later on Thursday 2026-09-24 at 14:42 JST, web-traffic fired due to an external search-engine crawler hitting public business pages. Traffic was elevated to about 3.4x the same hour last week, but requests returned all 2xx and backend services remained healthy. First move: no action. Logged a ticket for Aiko about crawler limits to decide if we want stricter rate limiting on public profiles.
- The Sunday payout job ran at 23:00 JST and finished in 39 minutes, processing scheduled business payouts normally across payments without manual intervention or delayed batches.
- As planned on the schedule, api and payments move to Shipyard, the new deploy pipeline, today (2026-09-28); the platform team posts the Shipyard page today. Nothing else changes for on-call this week.

## 3. Service status

- web: elevated traffic and one replaced node on us-east on Thursday, as detailed above; otherwise normal across all regions.
- api: normal throughout the week; scheduled migration to Shipyard begins today.
- payments: normal; the Sunday payout job completed smoothly in 39 minutes, and Shipyard migration starts today.
- notifier: normal with no alerts, queue backlogs, or provider drops.

## 4. Notes for the incoming on-call

- Watch for the platform team to publish the Shipyard documentation page today. Remember that api and payments move to Shipyard today (2026-09-28), but our daily operational duties remain the same since nothing else changes for on-call this week.
- Keep an eye on memory usage across web instances in us-east via the metrics tool to ensure the memory exhaustion seen on Thursday was an isolated instance issue rather than a wider leak.
- Follow up with Aiko on the crawler limit ticket if public crawl volume climbs again during peak daytime hours.
- Since I am covering back-to-back shifts following the swap with Daniel, I will acknowledge the handover in #inc-live directly.

## 5. Sign-off

Signed off by Leo (payments) at 09:00 JST on 2026-09-28. Writing "taken" in #inc-live to open the new shift.

# payments: notes for on-call

Last updated: 2026-02-02  
Owner: Mei (payments)  

Mei maintains this operational runbook page for the SRE rotation covering the payments service. Keep these operational notes handy when evaluating issues during shifts across ap-northeast, us-east, and eu-west.

## Duplicate capture on 63 bookings

On 2026-01-14, we ran into an issue where the capture call to stripe timed out from our side. The capture call to stripe was retried after a timeout and both captures went through, leading to duplicate capture on 63 bookings on 2026-01-14. This resulted in double billing across those specific appointments before our team detected the discrepancy in the logs.

Leo added an idempotency key to the capture call on 2026-01-15 to ensure that network timeouts on the provider interface do not cause double execution again. Mei's team refunded the second charge the same day to make sure the affected customer balances were reconciled cleanly.

When you see this on call:
- If double captures or unexpected double line items appear in records, read logs in the log search tool to check if the idempotency key was dropped or bypassed.
- If money moved incorrectly, page owner so Mei's team can review transactions and issue necessary refunds.

## Weekly payout schedule

The weekly payout job runs on Sunday at 23:00 JST and usually takes about 38 minutes. This process settles balances earned by businesses such as salons, clinics, and tutors using Sorrel. 

Because the job handles substantial database read and write volume while contacting external card networks, background load on payments will stay elevated for the entire duration of the run. 

Points to remember regarding payout execution:
- The weekly payout job runs on Sunday at 23:00 JST and usually takes about 38 minutes, so expect resource graphs on the "Sorrel / payments" board to show persistent load during that window.
- The job touches balance ledgers sequentially, meaning brief processing spikes around 23:00 JST are typical behavior.

When you see this on call:
- When payout task timers or elevated queue depths alert close to Sunday midnight JST, check whether the job has exceeded its standard window before treating it as stalled.
- If the job halts halfway through or throws unhandled exceptions during execution, read logs first, and page owner if money moved or payouts stalled halfway through.

## Daily refund batches

Refund batches run daily at 23:30 JST. This automated batch handles customer cancellation refunds and disputed appointment adjustments that have queued up over the previous twenty-four hours.

Key operational characteristics:
- Refund batches run daily at 23:30 JST, briefly competing with other late-evening queue workers in ap-northeast.
- The job aggregates pending return requests and sends them in structured batches directly downstream to stripe.
- Failures inside a batch are isolated so that an error on an individual refund does not abort the remaining executions in the queue.

When you see this on call:
- When queue latency blips occur around 23:30 JST, read logs to confirm that the refund batches run daily at 23:30 JST without dropping database connections.
- If a batch reports unrecoverable transaction corruption, page owner to avoid duplicate accounting entries.

## Provider webhook delivery behavior

Webhooks from the card provider can arrive late, out of order, or more than once; payments is built to handle all three, so a few retries are not an incident. The ingest pipelines store events idempotently and process lifecycle state changes based on event timestamps rather than arrival order.

Network hiccups between stripe edge servers and our cloudflare or aws ingress endpoints regularly cause delayed deliveries or multiple retry deliveries of identical event payloads.

Operational points:
- Webhooks from the card provider can arrive late, out of order, or more than once; payments is built to handle all three, so a few retries are not an incident.
- Deduplication prevents duplicate accounting events when redundant events hit webhooks concurrently.

When you see this on call:
- When webhook retry alerts trigger in low numbers, no action is needed if payloads are acknowledged normally on subsequent attempts.
- If webhooks fail completely across all endpoints, check provider status before assuming our ingest nodes are down.

— Mei

# notifier: things we learned the hard way

Last updated: 2026-03-09  
Owner: Tom (notifier)  

## Maintenance

Tom keeps this page for the notifier service. The on-call rotation uses it when queue depth or delivery alerts fire for email and SMS.

## Sending-domain switch and the suppression list

After the sending-domain switch on 2026-02-24, sendgrid's suppression list picked up 2,312 addresses from soft bounces during the switch, and sendgrid stopped sending to them. Yuki checked they were valid and removed them from the suppression list on 2026-02-26.

When you see drops on known good customer addresses after domain work:
- check provider before assuming the application dropped them silently.
- check the suppression list directly in sendgrid to see if addresses were added during cutovers.
- read logs in sorrel-prod-* to confirm whether the worker received an acceptance or an outright bounce from the provider.
- if an address is suppressed on their side, notifier will not attempt redelivery on its own.

## Nightly reminder batch volume

The nightly reminder batch (02:00 to 04:00 JST) regularly pushes queue depth past 1,000; check delivered per minute before treating it as a stall.

During this window, clinics, salons, and tutors have their next-day slots queued all at once. The backlog is expected behavior rather than a broken consumer:
- do not page owner merely because the backlog crosses four digits between 02:00 and 04:00 JST.
- open the metrics tool and check delivered per minute across the workers.
- if delivered per minute remains steady and workers are draining messages, choose no action and let the batch clear.
- if delivered per minute drops to zero while the queue sits above 1,000, read logs to see if workers are stuck or encountering errors.

## Queue separation for confirmations and reminders

Email confirmations and SMS reminders use separate queues.

Because these channels and message types do not share a single pipeline, backpressure in one does not directly block the other:
- an incident involving email delivery does not imply SMS traffic is halted.
- when email confirmations back up during daytime booking spikes, SMS reminders continue moving through their own queue.
- check provider status for both sendgrid and twilio separately when triaging broader notification delays.
- read logs for the specific worker group tied to the affected queue rather than treating the service as a single pipe.

## Reminder deduplication keys

Every reminder carries a dedupe key, reminder:<booking id>:<date>; notifier drops a message whose key it has seen in the last 24 hours.

This safeguards recipients from duplicate alerts when upstream schedulers resend booking batches or when retries occur:
- when api or batch jobs re-enqueue the same reminder run, notifier drops a message whose key it has seen in the last 24 hours without raising an error.
- if a business reports that a customer did not receive a second reminder after an update on the same day, read logs to inspect whether the dedupe key reminder:<booking id>:<date> was already recorded.
- if duplicate sends are suspected, check the logs for this key pattern to see if the drop logic executed as intended.
- do not alter dedupe keys manually during an incident without consulting Tom or Yuki.

## On-call summary

When notifier triggers an alert, determine which queue is affected before taking any disruptive step. If the nightly reminder batch is running between 02:00 and 04:00 JST, check delivered per minute in the metrics tool before assuming the worker pool has failed. If delivery stops entirely across third-party endpoints, check provider dashboards for sendgrid and twilio, then read logs to verify worker state.

# web: odd things we keep seeing

Last updated: 2026-07-13  
Owner: Aiko (web)  

## Maintenance

This page is maintained by Aiko and the web engineering team to track quirks that recur on the web service. We write these notes down so people working secondary shifts or holding the paging tool do not spend an hour rediscovering known oddities across our regions in ap-northeast, us-east, and eu-west.

## Rare kanji rendering boxes on booking pages

Tofu on the booking page in June 2026: customer names with rare kanji (for example 髙 or 﨑) rendered as empty boxes, because the subset web font left out those glyphs. Priya added a fallback to the full Noto Sans JP font on 2026-06-11.

* The problem was particularly visible on salon and clinic confirmation screens where end users entered family names containing un-subsetted characters.
* We traced the missing characters through the browser inspection tool before realizing the asset bundle was aggressively trimmed during build steps.
* Priya patched the stylesheet stack directly to pull the wider font when the primary bundle encounters an unmapped character code.
* When you see this on call, verify whether the browser is loading the fallback font and no action is required unless a new unmapped glyph set appears outside Japanese names.

## Crawler bursts tripping traffic alerts

Search-engine crawler bursts on public business pages trip web-traffic a few times a month; they are harmless when 5xx and page load stay flat.

* Bot fleets hitting business profile directories periodically generate noticeable step increases in inbound request counts across public endpoints.
* These automated spikes regularly show up on the metrics tool during off-peak hours and sometimes trigger automated traffic thresholds on the "Sorrel / web" board.
* The web app handles the read-only rendering without stressing downstream dependencies, provided the database caches held by api absorb the tenant queries properly.
* When you see this on call, check the metrics tool to confirm error rates and response latencies remain unaffected; if metrics are healthy, take no action and log it in the shift notes.

## Safari service worker persistence after releases

Safari keeps the old service worker longer than other browsers; after a release, support can ask a customer to reload twice.

* Following a routine update using the deploy tool, we periodically hear from Hana that customers on Apple devices still run older client bundles.
* The caching layer in WebKit hangs onto active worker registrations significantly longer than Chromium or Gecko runtimes, even when lifecycle headers prompt an update.
* This discrepancy occasionally produces minor script errors or stale form behavior on the admin tool and booking panels right after fresh code lands.
* When you see this on call, point support to the known browser workaround so Hana can advise the user without escalating a bug to the team.

## Static asset invalidation via cloudflare

The cloudflare edge serves most static files; a purge normally finishes in about a minute.

* Our frontend bundle assets, icons, and public business stylesheets rely on external caching to prevent load from saturating hosting instances on aws.
* Whenever a quick hotfix goes through and stale assets linger across edge locations, clearing cache tags or URLs via cloudflare restores freshness swiftly.
* Edge nodes reliably drop their cached objects within sixty seconds, making this a predictable operation during routine asset updates.
* When you see this on call, check provider if static asset updates appear delayed across edge locations after a recent push.

-- Aiko
